summary:

The job-board Actor's onlyNewSinceLastRun option emits postings unseen by an earlier run with the same query shape. The first run returns everything.

title: BYOL Windows Server on a VPS: licensing done right
summary:
"BYOL" shows up on every Windows VPS page and rarely gets explained. Here is the whole thing, honestly: what the licence is, why the image starts as Evaluation, how to activate, how to switch editions without reinstalling, and which keys are actually allowed on a rented server.

Why the image is Evaluation

When you deploy a Windows plan, the machine boots Windows Server 2022 Standard (Desktop Experience) from a clean image — with the virtio drivers and guest agent already in place, so RDP and the console work out of the box. That image is the Evaluation edition.

Evaluation is a genuine, fully functional Windows Server — it just isn't licensed for production, and it runs on a timer. It exists so you can set the server up, test that your software runs, and decide it's the right box before you activate. title: Vercel Functions now support request bodies up to 20MiB
summary:
Vercel Functions now accept inbound request bodies up to 20MiB, up from 4.5MB, in Public Beta.

To turn this on, set the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY=1 environment variable. The opt-in applies to the whole project in the environment where you set it, so you can test the larger limit on preview before enabling it in production. It requires the project's functions to use the performance memory setting of 4GB. It applies to functions on the Node.js, Python, and Bun runtimes, and to Routing Middleware. Functions and Routing Middleware on the Edge runtime keep the 4.5MB cap and return 413 on oversize bodies, so moving them onto the larger limit means switching to the Node.js runtime with runtime: 'nodejs', or proxy.ts in Next.js.

title: Checking Borat quotes with Python's difflib: Wikiquote vs the film transcript
summary:
Most movie quote pages copy each other. One site types a line from memory, another copies it, and soon "Very nice!" is followed by words nobody in the film ever said.

For our Borat quotes page we used a simple rule: a film line goes on the page only if two separate texts agree on it. The first is Wikiquote. The second is a transcript of the film. A short Python script decides whether they agree.

Of the 97 Borat lines the script checked, 74 passed. This post covers how it decides, why the other 23 failed, and a mistake the check missed that I found while writing this.

The two witnesses

Witness 1: Wikiquote. We fetch each film's page as wikitext (action=raw) and parse it into JSON: one record per line, with the speaker and the film. The wording on our page is copied from this file, never retyped.

title: 5 automation workflows that save small teams 20+ hours every week
summary:
The typical small business owner loses 14 hours a week to tasks that software could do faster, better, and without a single sick day. It never shows up as waste on the income statement. It vanishes into payroll, written off as "just doing the job."

Consider a 5-person service business paying an average of $25 an hour. It spends $10,000 to $15,000 a month on administrative overhead alone, and most of that can be automated. The figure doesn't come from big, memorable tasks. It comes from two-minute chores that repeat fifty times a week: manually logging a lead into a CRM, sending the same welcome email with one name swapped, building a weekly report from three different spreadsheets, or chasing an invoice that has sat unpaid for eleven days.

None of these is a complex problem. They're repetitive ones, and repetitive problems with predictable inputs and outputs are exactly what no-code automation handles well in 2026.

title: We shipped a browser game to the Microsoft Store as a $0.99 app
summary:
Our games are small HTML5 titles that already run in any browser. The Microsoft Store accepts Progressive Web Apps, so we tried selling two of them there for $0.99. Both passed certification on the first try. Here is what it took.

1. Make the game a real PWA

The Store packages a website, so the website has to behave like an app:

  • a manifest.webmanifest with name, icons (192 and 512 px), display: fullscreen and start_url: ./;
  • a service worker that caches every file of the game, so it starts with no network at all. We version the cache with the build time and delete old caches on activate;
  • no dependence on anything external to start. If an SDK script fails to load offline, the game must boot anyway.

We tested the last point the boring way: load the page once, switch the browser to offline, reload. If the canvas draws, the app will work on a plane.

title: Making a 3D glass portfolio fast
summary:
Five changes took this portfolio from about 46 fps mid-page to 60 fps in the hero and the mid fifties lower down. It removed backdrop blur over the canvas, dropped blend modes, froze the orbs, gave the WebGL field adaptive quality, and deferred its scripts.

Why was the first version slow?

The site runs five apps as live demos inside phone and laptop frames. Behind them a Three.js field draws 2,600 dust particles, a 150-node synaptic lattice with travelling pulses, and holographic shards. The canvas changes on every frame.

The first version held up in the hero and then dropped to about 46 fps mid-page on a mid laptop. The WebGL code was not the main cost. The damage came from the CSS layered on top of the canvas.

title: An eye test in the browser: turning CSS pixels into millimetres with a bank card
summary:
A distance eye test has one hard requirement: the letter on the screen has to be a known physical size, at a known distance. The browser gives you neither. A CSS pixel isn't a physical unit, there's no API that reports millimetres, and devicePixelRatio tells you about device pixels, not about the size of the glass.

We built a free eye test that runs in a browser tab anyway (anpheros.com/eye-test). This post covers how it gets a physical size out of a web page, the maths that turns a distance into a letter height, and where the precision quietly runs out.

Step 1: a ruler everyone carries

Bank cards, ID cards and most loyalty cards share one format, ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1: 85.60 × 53.98 mm. That's a physical reference almost everyone has in reach.

title: The Comment That Ruined My Thursday
summary:
09:12. I open the pull request and there it is, three words under a line of my code, in red.

"This is wrong."

No line number beyond the one it sits on. No "because". No "try this instead". Just the three words, and a name beside them I recognise from the team list, and a little grey timestamp that says it arrived at 08:47, twenty-five minutes before I got to my desk.

I read it again. Then I read it a third time, slower, as if the extra words might be hiding between the three that are there. They are not.

The line it sits on is mine. It sorts a list of invoices by date, and I wrote it on Tuesday afternoon, in a hurry, because the dashboard needed it and the afternoon was already gone. I remember writing it. I remember feeling clever about it for about four seconds, which is the usual length of time I feel clever about anything I write.
